ann_114.original: The linear backbone of the model: direct edges from z-scored inputs to the output score, so each weight is in logit per sd of its input. The outcome is the low-income class (income of at most $50k), so a negative weight lowers the predicted probability of low income. The largest direct weights lower it for capital gain (-2.66), husbands (-0.93), years of education (-0.78 per sd of education-num), wives (-0.53), age (-0.36), hours worked (-0.36), civilian marriage (-0.31) and capital loss (-0.27); they raise it for never-married people (0.24), other-service occupations (0.25) and work without pay (0.34). Prediction, checked by self-probes on the typical case (a married male high-school graduate in private work): in the whole model the predicted probability of low income falls from 74% at 25 years to 50% at 65 years, from 79% at 20 hours a week to 54% at 60 hours, and from 68% at education-num 9 on the 1-16 scale to 38% at 13 on the 1-16 scale (the education category held at high-school graduate). Several inputs also feed a hidden part (capital gain, wife, executive or managerial, without pay, Japan); their whole-model effect is the direct edge plus that part, given in the part's hypothesis. The Netherlands level of native country has a direct edge of -0.34 but 0 training rows, so on the training data it acts as a constant. Switching the whole linear part off (its exit held at its training mean) lowers training AUC from 0.906 to 0.743: this part carries most of the model's ranking.
ann_114.proposed: A weighted sum of the inputs: through it alone, higher capital gains lower the predicted chance steadily (from about 68% to about 16% at 6849 US dollars), more education lowers it in stages, and being never married raises it to about 96%.

ann_115.original: A capital-gain threshold: above a capital gain of a few thousand dollars the model adds a second downward push on the predicted probability of low income, on top of the direct capital-gain edge (weight -2.66 logit per sd). Prediction, self-probed on the typical case: the hinge is closed at 4300 US dollars (pre-activation -0.0032) and open at 4350 US dollars (value 0.0045); through this part it adds -0.32 logit at 10000 US dollars and -0.88 at 20000 US dollars. In the whole model the typical case's predicted probability of low income falls from 68% at 0 US dollars to 25% at 5000 US dollars and 4% at 10000 US dollars; most of that fall is the direct edge, the hinge steepens it. The hinge acts on 2215 training rows (low-income rate 15.2%), where its mean contribution is -0.77 logit; 1070 rows have a positive capital gain below the threshold, where the hinge is closed. A copy of the same hinge also feeds the female gate with a very small weight (see that part). Switching the hinge off changes training AUC from 0.9056 to 0.9054.
ann_115.proposed: For people with large capital gains a second downward push: it acts on 2215 of 39073 training people, and for the typical one it lowers the predicted chance from about 4% to about 3%.

ann_116.original: A gate that is open for women and for men in private household service, and closed for other men; when open it raises the predicted probability of low income. It is open on 12971 training rows. Of the 12959 women, the share with the gate open is 1.000 (0 women with it closed); 12 men have it open, all in private household service (0 men in other occupations open, and 0 of the 12 men in private household service closed). The male part of the gate is fitted to 12 rows. Through this part, women gain 0.62 logit on average. Self-probe (a never-married person not in a family, otherwise typical): an administrative or clerical woman gets 0.58 logit through the gate and the same man's gate is closed (pre-activation -1.17), so the whole-model predicted probability is 98% for her against 97% for him; in private household service the gate gives 3.62 for a woman and 2.03 for a man. The capital-gain hinge enters with a tiny weight: for the same woman the gate value moves from 0.676 at 0 US dollars to 0.598 at 99999 US dollars, so it stays open. Switching the gate off lowers training AUC from 0.9056 to 0.9039, the largest loss of any hidden part.
ann_116.proposed: A shift that acts on 12971 training people, nearly all of them women, and raises their predicted chance; private household service raises it more for women than for men, from about 68% to about 96% for a typical man.

ann_120.original: Separated people get a higher predicted probability of low income than otherwise identical divorced people. ann_121.original: Working without pay pushes the predicted probability of low income to near certainty. The unit is open on every row (active fraction 1.0), a linear term in the without-pay indicator; because that indicator is rare, its z-scored value for the people who have it is very large, and so is the push. Fitted to 17 training rows, whose mean predicted probability is 1.000 and whose low-income rate is 0.88. Self-probe on the typical case: with work without pay the unit contributes 44.5 logit (from its training mean) against -0.02 with private work, and the direct without-pay edge (0.34 per sd) pushes the same way; the whole-model predicted probability is 1.0000 against 68%.

ann_122.original: For people born in Japan this unit nearly cancels the direct Japan edge. The direct edge lowers the score (-0.19 logit per sd); this always-on unit (active fraction 1.0) raises it by about as much. On the 68 training rows born in Japan the unit's mean contribution is 4.69 logit. ann_124.original: The model predicts the probability of the low-income class (income of at most $50k) as a sigmoid of a mostly linear score: the direct linear terms plus nine hidden parts, added on the logit scale. The hidden parts are shifts for particular groups (women and men in private household service, wives, executives and managers, missing work class, separated, without pay, Japan), a capital-gain threshold, and one dead unit. Prediction, tested by ablation: switching all nine hidden parts off at once changes training AUC from 0.9056 to 0.9025, while switching the linear part off lowers it to 0.7427. The three largest parts by AUC loss are the linear part, the female gate (AUC without it 0.9039) and the Japan unit (AUC without it 0.9049, because it cancels a large direct edge). On the training split (39073 rows) the low-income rate is 76.1% and the mean predicted probability 76.2%; the typical case (a married male high-school graduate in private work) gets 68%.
ann_124.proposed: The model adds up ten parts: a weighted sum of the inputs and nine shifts for particular groups. For a typical person it predicts a chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) of about 68%; higher capital gains lower it steadily to about 14% at 6849 US dollars.

parts.original_hypothesis: The model predicts the probability of the low-income class (income of at most $50k) as a sigmoid of a mostly linear score: the direct linear terms plus nine hidden parts, added on the logit scale. The hidden parts are shifts for particular groups (women and men in private household service, wives, executives and managers, missing work class, separated, without pay, Japan), a capital-gain threshold, and one dead unit. Prediction, tested by ablation: switching all nine hidden parts off at once changes training AUC from 0.9056 to 0.9025, while switching the linear part off lowers it to 0.7427. The three largest parts by AUC loss are the linear part, the female gate (AUC without it 0.9039) and the Japan unit (AUC without it 0.9049, because it cancels a large direct edge). On the training split (39073 rows) the low-income rate is 76.1% and the mean predicted probability 76.2%; the typical case (a married male high-school graduate in private work) gets 68%.

parts.name: direct_linear_terms
parts.original_hypothesis: The linear backbone of the model: direct edges from z-scored inputs to the output score, so each weight is in logit per sd of its input. The outcome is the low-income class (income of at most $50k), so a negative weight lowers the predicted probability of low income. The largest direct weights lower it for capital gain (-2.66), husbands (-0.93), years of education (-0.78 per sd of education-num), wives (-0.53), age (-0.36), hours worked (-0.36), civilian marriage (-0.31) and capital loss (-0.27); they raise it for never-married people (0.24), other-service occupations (0.25) and work without pay (0.34). Prediction, checked by self-probes on the typical case (a married male high-school graduate in private work): in the whole model the predicted probability of low income falls from 74% at 25 years to 50% at 65 years, from 79% at 20 hours a week to 54% at 60 hours, and from 68% at education-num 9 on the 1-16 scale to 38% at 13 on the 1-16 scale (the education category held at high-school graduate). Several inputs also feed a hidden part (capital gain, wife, executive or managerial, without pay, Japan); their whole-model effect is the direct edge plus that part, given in the part's hypothesis. The Netherlands level of native country has a direct edge of -0.34 but 0 training rows, so on the training data it acts as a constant. Switching the whole linear part off (its exit held at its training mean) lowers training AUC from 0.906 to 0.743: this part carries most of the model's ranking.

The unit is open on every row (active fraction 1.0), a linear term in the without-pay indicator; because that indicator is rare, its z-scored value for the people who have it is very large, and so is the push.
